pages.metaTitle: Bitcoin, Ethereum and Solana | Rezo Shmertz
pages.description: Bitcoin behaves like digital gold while Ethereum and Solana resemble productive economic layers. Rezo Shmertz explains why the systems are complementary.
pages.h1: Bitcoin Doesn't Compete with Ethereum and Solana
pages.lead: Treating Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Solana as interchangeable assets hides the different economic jobs their systems are designed to perform.

visual.alt: Original article illustration showing Bitcoin with gold and Ethereum and Solana on oil barrels

paras: Bitcoin's singular monetary proposition is scarcity, security, and settlement assurance. Its economy is optimized around extracting, securing, and holding a monetary asset.
Ethereum and Solana are productive layers. Their value is tied to applications, staking, transaction demand, stablecoins, tokenized assets, and the economic activity that can be built on top.
The relevant success metrics are therefore not identical.
list: Bitcoin: institutional adoption, monetary credibility, security, and settlement volume
Ethereum: fees, staking, composability, developer activity, and application value
Solana: throughput, cost efficiency, consumer applications, payments, and high-frequency markets

paras: Gold miners and oil producers participate in different economies. In the same way, a monetary store of value does not need to win the application-platform race, and a productive smart-contract network does not need to become digital gold.
The more useful question is not which one eliminates the others, but how large each specialized economy can become.

contextParas: Bitcoin, Ethereum and Solana raise different questions about money and digital infrastructure. This essay separates monetary scarcity from demand for computation, and considers why those roles need different measures of value. It is an argument about how to compare systems, not a ranking of their tokens.

The AI Money study approaches a related question by comparing classified AI responses across four monetary functions. For Rezo Shmertz's broader views on Bitcoin and open financial infrastructure, see What I Believe.

pages.description: Self-custody removes one class of exchange risk, but credible perpetual markets also require transparent execution, liquidations, incentives, and solvency.
pages.h1: Non-Custodial Isn't Enough: Why Perp DEXs Need Transparency
pages.lead: Self-custody solves custody risk. It does not, by itself, make a derivatives market transparent, solvent, or fair.

visual.alt: Original cover of Rezo Shmertz's article on perpetual DEX transparency

sections.h2: One risk layer is not the whole market
paras: A non-custodial venue can let traders retain control of assets while leaving other mechanisms difficult to verify. Execution priority, oracle design, liquidation rules, insurance funds, market-maker incentives, and the treatment of bad debt still determine whether the system is credible.
The important distinction is between control of collateral and transparency of the complete market structure.
A serious perpetual market should make the rules legible before stress arrives and make outcomes auditable after it does.
list: How orders are matched and prioritized
How prices and funding rates are formed
How liquidations and bad debt are handled
How market makers and token incentives are compensated
Whether reserves and risk parameters can be independently checked

paras: Self-custody is necessary progress, but the stronger standard is verifiable market structure. Users should not have to exchange custodial opacity for protocol opacity.
The market earns trust when its risk, execution, and incentives can be inspected rather than merely promised.

contextParas: Self-custody is one part of decentralized finance. The operation of a trading venue raises separate questions about execution, liquidations, solvency and the information available to participants. This essay examines those market-structure questions in perpetual futures, where control of assets alone does not explain how the wider system works.

Related writing on Bitcoin, Ethereum and Solana considers the different roles of financial networks. Rezo Shmertz's working principles connect these subjects to openness, infrastructure and incentives.

pages.metaTitle: Bitcoin and Quantum Risk | Rezo Shmertz
pages.description: Bitcoin's quantum risk has an unknowable deadline. Rezo Shmertz argues for address hygiene, post-quantum research, and upgrade optionality without panic.
pages.h1: The Quantum Threat to Bitcoin: We Can't Predict the Timeline
pages.lead: The hard problem is not choosing one confident quantum deadline. It is preparing for asymmetric risk when the deadline cannot be known.

visual.alt: Original cover of Rezo Shmertz's article on the quantum threat to Bitcoin

sections.h2: Two rigorous views, one missing variable
paras: Estimates of Bitcoin's quantum exposure differ because they count vulnerable coins differently and assume different trajectories for quantum computing. A linear projection can imply decades; investment and breakthrough-driven projections can imply much less time.
Both approaches face the same limitation: breakthrough technologies do not follow a schedule we can forecast reliably.

Moving too slowly risks catastrophic loss if usable quantum systems arrive early. Moving too quickly risks deploying immature cryptography and creating a new vulnerability in the attempt to solve the old one.
list: Stop address reuse and improve address hygiene
Monitor algorithmic breakthroughs, not only qubit counts
Develop multiple upgrade and fallback paths
Avoid treating a speculative date as certainty

paras: Uncertainty is not permission to ignore the threat. It is also not a reason to rush untested cryptography.
Bitcoin can treat quantum computing as a tail risk with unclear timing: build optionality now, improve operational hygiene, and preserve the ability to migrate deliberately when evidence changes.

contextParas: Quantum computing raises a different question from Bitcoin's day-to-day price movements: how a monetary network prepares for a security risk with an uncertain timeline. This essay focuses on that uncertainty, the choices available to holders and developers, and the difference between acknowledging a risk and claiming to know when it will arrive.
For a separate view of market history, the Bitcoin Cycle Tracker presents cycle timing and drawdown context. It does not model quantum risk. Further essays are collected in Writings.

pages.metaTitle: AI Agents and Investment Judgment | Rezo Shmertz
pages.description: Rezo Shmertz on what remains scarce when AI makes analysis abundant: judgment, trust, distribution, responsibility, and the ability to act.
pages.h1: Warren Buffett, AI Agents, and Why Your Edge Was Never About Thinking
pages.lead: When machine intelligence makes analysis cheaper, the durable edge moves toward judgment, trust, distribution, and the ability to act.

visual.alt: Original cover of Rezo Shmertz's article on Warren Buffett, AI agents and market advantages

paras: AI agents compress the cost of collecting information, comparing scenarios, and producing competent analysis. That changes the value of thinking as a standalone advantage: an answer is less scarce when thousands of systems can generate one on demand.
The harder advantage is deciding which question deserves attention, which evidence deserves trust, and which conclusion is important enough to act on.

Judgment carries responsibility. Trust takes time to earn. Distribution determines whether an idea reaches capital and institutions. Action requires permission, relationships, temperament, and a willingness to live with the result.
Those constraints do not disappear when intelligence becomes abundant. They become more visible.

The Buffett lesson was never simply that one person could process more information than the market. It was that temperament, incentives, patience, reputation, and capital allocation compound together.
AI can strengthen the analytical layer. It does not automatically supply the conviction or institutional trust required to deploy capital through a full cycle.

contextParas: As AI makes analysis more widely available, this essay asks where an investor's advantage comes from. Its focus is on the work beyond producing an answer: judgment, trust, distribution, responsibility and the ability to act.

The BR Labs episode on AI and trust explores related questions about builders and institutional adoption. The AI Money study examines a different application of AI, comparing model responses across monetary functions.
